title: Advanced Querying & Syntaxes
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs routinely test subqueries, CTEs, window functions, and conditional aggregation as the leap from basic SELECT/JOIN to analytical SQL.

phases.goal: Establish what subqueries, CTEs, and window functions are and how they differ from basic retrieval and GROUP BY aggregation.

must_hit.point: A subquery is a query nested inside another query; non-correlated ones can be evaluated independently, while correlated ones reference the outer query.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says nested query, and contrasts independent (run once) vs outer-row-dependent evaluation.

must_hit.point: A CTE (WITH) is a temporary named result set that exists only for the duration of the query, used to replace deeply nested subqueries with readable top-to-bottom code.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions WITH, temporary/named result, query-scoped lifetime, readability over nested subqueries.

must_hit.point: A window function computes over a related set of rows via OVER but retains every input row, unlike GROUP BY which collapses rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts meat-grinder GROUP BY collapse vs magnifying-glass window that keeps row identity.

must_hit.point: Subqueries can appear in WHERE, FROM (derived table), and SELECT (scalar: exactly one row and one column).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists clause placements and notes SELECT-list subqueries must be scalar.

probes: What is a CTE, and how is a window function different from a GROUP BY aggregate?

hints.1: Think about whether rows survive in the result and whether the inner query can stand alone.
hints.2: CTE = WITH named temp result; window = OVER calculation without collapsing rows.
hints.3: Non-correlated subquery runs independently; correlated references outer columns; window keeps every row while attaching a partition-scoped value.

phases.goal: Explain correlated execution, recursive CTE iteration, OVER anatomy, ranking ties, navigation functions, and default frames.

must_hit.point: A correlated subquery has a row-by-row dependency: the inner query cannot run independently and must conceptually execute once per outer candidate row.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks outer row → substitute outer key into inner AVG → compare → repeat for next row.

must_hit.point: A recursive CTE needs RECURSIVE, an anchor member, and a recursive member combined with UNION or UNION ALL; the self-reference uses only the immediately preceding iteration's working set until an iteration returns zero rows.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes anchor (e.g. CEO), then join previous working set for next level, stop when nothing new.

must_hit.point: OVER may include PARTITION BY (resets per group), ORDER BY (sequence; required for ranking and running totals), and a frame clause (sliding boundary within the partition).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three OVER sub-clauses and what each controls.

must_hit.point: For tied salaries like 100k, 100k, 90k: ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3; RANK gives 1, 1, 3; DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the three tie behaviors with those exact rank sequences.

must_hit.point: With ORDER BY in OVER, the default frame becomes ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (running total); without ORDER BY the frame is the entire partition.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why SUM(... ORDER BY hire_date) is cumulative and cites the default frame.

must_hit.point: LAG and LEAD pull values from offset rows relative to the current row; FIRST_VALUE pulls the first value in the window.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives prev/next salary via LAG/LEAD and top earner via FIRST_VALUE.

probes: Walk through how a correlated subquery runs row by row, then how a recursive OrgChart CTE iterates from the anchor.
For salaries 100k, 100k, 90k, what do ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK return, and what is the default frame when ORDER BY is in OVER?

hints.1: Start with one outer employee, then the anchor vs recursive member of WITH RECURSIVE.
hints.2: Correlated = re-run inner per outer row; recursive = previous working set only; ranking = gaps vs no gaps; ORDER BY shrinks the default frame to current row.
hints.3: Inner AVG uses outer dept_id each time; OrgChart grows CEO→VPs→Directors until empty; ties: 1,2,3 / 1,1,3 / 1,1,2; default frame with ORDER BY is UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW.

phases.goal: Compare EXISTS vs IN, correlated rewrites, and portable CASE vs Postgres FILTER for pivots.

must_hit.point: EXISTS checks whether a subquery returns any rows and can short-circuit on the first match; IN checks membership against a fully generated list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts short-circuit existence vs building the full ID list for membership.

must_hit.point: When performance matters, a correlated subquery should usually be rewritten as a JOIN or a window function because it may re-execute the inner query once per outer row (e.g. on a table with 10 million rows).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Flags row-by-row cost and names JOIN / window rewrite as the usual fix.

must_hit.point: Postgres has no native PIVOT keyword; everyday pivoting uses conditional aggregation—portable SUM(CASE WHEN ...) or cleaner SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE ...).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says no PIVOT, then CASE vs FILTER; may mention crosstab as extension-only alternative.

probes: When would you prefer EXISTS over IN, and when would you rewrite a correlated subquery?
How do you pivot quarters into columns in PostgreSQL without a PIVOT keyword?

hints.1: Think short-circuit existence vs full lists, and rewrite cost of correlation.
hints.2: EXISTS stops early; correlated often becomes JOIN/window; pivot = aggregate + condition per column.
hints.3: EXISTS short-circuits; avoid correlated on huge tables—use JOIN/window; use SUM(CASE...) or SUM() FILTER (WHERE quarter = 'Q1') etc.

phases.goal: Apply advanced syntax to common interview tasks: above-dept-average employees, org charts, rankings, running/moving aggregates, null-safe defaults, and crosstabs.

must_hit.point: Find employees above their own department average with a correlated subquery on matching dept_id, or equivalently with a window AVG(... PARTITION BY dept_id).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes salary > dept AVG via correlation or OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id).

must_hit.point: Build an org chart from manager_id with a recursive CTE: anchor where manager_id IS NULL, then join employees to the prior OrgChart level and track depth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names RECURSIVE, anchor (no manager), recursive join on manager_id, depth increment.

must_hit.point: Use COALESCE for first non-null defaults (e.g. COALESCE(bonus, 0)) and NULLIF to avoid divide-by-zero (e.g. total / NULLIF(count, 0)).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States first-non-null COALESCE and NULLIF equal-args → NULL for safe division.

must_hit.point: Express a moving average with an explicit frame such as ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Writes or describes AVG over ORDER BY with that 2-preceding frame.

probes: Write or outline SQL for employees above department average, a recursive org chart, and a quarter revenue pivot.
How would you default null bonuses and safely divide totals by counts that might be zero?

hints.1: Pick correlated or window for dept average; WITH RECURSIVE for hierarchy; CASE/FILTER for pivot.
hints.2: Outer salary vs inner AVG on same dept_id; anchor CEO then children; SUM with CASE/FILTER per quarter; COALESCE/NULLIF for nulls.
hints.3: Correlated AVG by dept_id or AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id); RECURSIVE OrgChart; SUM(revenue) FILTER (WHERE quarter = 'Q1'); COALESCE(bonus, 0) and total / NULLIF(count, 0).

tradeoffs.topic: Correlated subquery vs JOIN or Window Function
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Correlated subqueries are clear for per-row comparisons (e.g. salary vs own dept average) but imply re-running the inner query per outer row and can grind to a halt on large tables (e.g. 10 million rows); prefer a JOIN to pre-aggregated stats or a window function when performance matters.

IN builds a membership list from the subquery then checks values; EXISTS only cares that any matching row exists and can short-circuit on the first match, which is especially efficient with correlated existence checks.

tradeoffs.topic: GROUP BY aggregation vs Window Functions
tradeoffs.strong_answer: GROUP BY collapses many rows into one aggregated result; window functions attach aggregate-like values over a partition/frame while keeping every input row in the result.

Both pivot row labels into columns via conditional aggregation; SUM(CASE WHEN ...) is portable standard SQL, while SUM(...) FILTER (WHERE ...) is the cleaner modern PostgreSQL form; crosstab() can pivot dynamically but needs the tablefunc extension.

ROW_NUMBER always assigns distinct sequential positions (ties broken arbitrarily); RANK shares rank on ties but leaves gaps; DENSE_RANK shares rank on ties with no gaps—e.g. for 100k, 100k, 90k → (1,2,3), (1,1,3), (1,1,2).

gotchas.trap: Using NOT IN when the subquery can return NULL (e.g. parent_id).
gotchas.correction: If even one subquery value is NULL, NOT IN becomes UNKNOWN (treated as false for filtering) and the query can return zero rows; use NOT EXISTS when NULLs are possible.

gotchas.trap: Expecting LAST_VALUE() with ORDER BY to return the last row of the partition.
gotchas.correction: With ORDER BY, the default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so LAST_VALUE often returns the current row; set ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING for the true partition end.

gotchas.trap: Assuming SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...) still averages/sums the entire partition.
gotchas.correction: Adding ORDER BY changes the default frame to UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW, producing a running total unless you override the frame.

gotchas.trap: Leaving a correlated subquery on a very large outer table for production.
gotchas.correction: Row-by-row re-execution (conceptually once per outer row, e.g. 10 million times) can destroy performance; rewrite with a JOIN or window function.
